titre: “Here I Stand”: The Phrase Luther May Never Have Said (1521)
accroche: Luther's most famous line at the Diet of Worms appears in no account from the day he is said to have spoken it.
contenu_vulgarise:
On April 18, 1521, before Emperor Charles V assembled in diet at Worms, Martin Luther refuses to retract his writings. His answer, as recorded in the accounts of the session, ends like this: “I cannot and will not recant anything, since it is neither safe nor right to go against conscience. May God help me. Amen.” That is the sentence, and not another, that the witnesses present that day report.

## A Sentence Added After the Fact

The formula that became famous (“Here I stand, I cannot do otherwise” (Hier stehe ich, ich kann nicht anders)) appears in none of these accounts taken at the time. It first emerges in printed editions of the Diet published shortly after the events. The turn of phrase is effective, sums up the spirit of his answer well, and Luther never disowned it, but no document contemporary with the session itself attests to it. It is probably a reconstruction, added by an editor or a witness writing from memory, not a quotation taken on the spot.

## What the Legend Gained by Becoming Sharper

The case is interesting less for what it reveals about Luther than for what it reveals about how a founding scene is manufactured. The short version is more striking to the ear, more quotable, easier to carve on a monument: the historian Roland Bainton even made it, in 1950, the title of his standard biography, *Here I Stand*. The sentence actually spoken, more legalistic and less theatrical, spoke of conscience and scriptural proof; the one we remember speaks of posture and solitary courage. Neither changes the outcome of the Diet: five weeks later, on May 25, 1521, Charles V issues the Edict of Worms, which places Luther under the ban of the Empire and forbids the circulation of his writings, a sanction the emperor had, so to speak, already decided on, since this hearing aimed only at obtaining a retraction before he cracked down.

The added sentence therefore changed nothing in the political outcome, but it has changed how the episode has been told for five centuries: a reasoned refusal, grounded in Scripture and reason, turned into a cry of solitary defiance in the face of the Empire. It caught on because it tells better the story people wanted to remember: which is never proof that it was said, only proof that it deserved to be.

quiz.question: What does the absence of “Here I stand” from the accounts taken at the time of the Diet of Worms show?
choix: That Luther lied about what he had really said to Charles V
That the formula was added after the fact, in printed editions
That the Diet of Worms never took place as it is told today
That Luther expressed himself only in writing, never before an assembly
quiz.explication: The accounts of April 18, 1521 give a more sober answer, centered on conscience and Scripture; the formula is still attributed to Luther without his having denied it, but nothing points to a lie, a fictitious diet, or a purely written statement.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What sanction does Charles V take against Luther five weeks after the Diet of Worms?
choix: The Edict of Worms, which places him under the ban of the Empire and forbids his writings
His immediate excommunication, pronounced by the emperor himself
The confiscation of all his property in Saxony
A trial for heresy before an imperial court
quiz_supplementaire.explication: On May 25, 1521, Charles V issues the Edict of Worms, which places Luther under the ban of the Empire and forbids the circulation of his writings.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Where does the phrase “Here I stand” first appear?
choix: In a private letter from Luther to a friend, written that same evening
In the printed editions of the Diet, published shortly after the events
In a sermon delivered by Luther years later
In the official minutes handed to Charles V
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The formula first emerges in the printed editions of the Diet published shortly after the events.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the historian Roland Bainton do with the apocryphal formula in 1950?
choix: He proves that it appears in a record that has been found
He attributes the phrase to a contemporary of Luther, not to Luther himself
He makes it the title of his standard biography of Luther
He removes it from all reissues of Luther's works
quiz_supplementaire.explication: In 1950, Roland Bainton makes the apocryphal formula the title of his standard biography of Luther, Here I Stand.
